questions.question: What are the key elements of a UML class diagram?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the visual language of class diagrams, essential for communicating object-oriented designs in interviews and documentation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing relationship arrows (especially inheritance vs interface implementation) or forgetting that class diagrams show structure, not runtime flow.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multiplicity numbers (1..*, 0..1) on associations and explain when you'd use composition (filled diamond) versus aggregation (hollow diamond) based on lifecycle ownership.

questions.direct_answer: A UML class diagram represents classes as boxes divided into three sections: name at the top, attributes in the middle, methods at the bottom. Relationships between classes are shown using different line styles: solid arrows for inheritance, dashed arrows for interface implementation, diamonds for composition/aggregation, and plain lines for association. Visibility markers like + (public) and - (private) prefix members.

answer_sections.content: In a UML class diagram, each class is a box with three sections: name at top, attributes in the middle showing type and visibility (+ public, - private, # protected), and methods at the bottom. Relationships use different arrow types: a solid arrowhead means inheritance ('extends'), a dashed arrowhead means implements an interface. A filled diamond shows composition — the containing class owns the contained one (ParkingLot has a filled diamond to ParkingFloor). A hollow diamond shows aggregation — weaker association. In LLD interviews, you don't need perfect UML syntax, but using these conventions communicates your design clearly. The key is showing the relationships correctly.

groups.heading: Solid arrow
groups.text: Inheritance — Car points to Vehicle meaning Car extends Vehicle.

groups.heading: Dashed arrow
groups.text: Implements or dependency — Car pointing to Payable means Car implements Payable.

groups.heading: Filled diamond
groups.text: Composition — ParkingLot has a filled diamond to ParkingFloor, meaning Floor can't exist without Lot.

groups.heading: Hollow diamond
groups.text: Aggregation — weaker ownership, like Department and Employee.

groups.heading: Plain line
groups.text: Association — ParkingLot references DisplayBoard but doesn't own it.

beats.text: candidates miss: perfect UML syntax matters less than clear communication. Interviewers care that you're showing the right relationships — not that your arrowheads are pixel-perfect.

speakable_v2.cap: Learn five symbols: inheritance arrow, implements dashed arrow, filled diamond, hollow diamond, and plain line. That covers 95% of what you'll draw in any LLD interview.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Class = **3-part box**: name, attributes, methods.
- Visibility: `+` public, `-` private, `#` protected.
- **Solid + hollow triangle** = inheritance; **dashed + hollow triangle** = implements.
- **Filled diamond** = composition; **hollow diamond** = aggregation; plain line = association.
- **Multiplicities** (1, \*) label how many on each end.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A UML class diagram captures the static structure of a design. Each class is drawn as a box split into three sections: the class name at the top, its attributes in the middle, and its methods at the bottom. In front of each attribute or method you put a visibility marker — a plus for public, a minus for private, and a hash for protected — so the diagram communicates access control at a glance.

But the boxes are only half the story; the lines between them carry just as much meaning, and that's where people slip. A solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the parent means inheritance, an is-a relationship via extends. A dashed line with a hollow triangle means a class implements an interface. A filled diamond means composition — strong ownership, where the part can't live without the whole, like a parking floor inside a lot. A hollow diamond means aggregation, a weaker ownership where the part can exist independently, like players in a team. And a plain line is a general association, meaning one class just uses or knows about another.

The last detail I'd mention is multiplicity — the little numbers at each end of a line, like one and star, that say a lot has one-to-many floors. So when I read or draw a class diagram, I'm reading the boxes for structure and the line styles and arrowheads for how the classes relate, because getting the arrowheads right is what proves you actually understand composition versus inheritance.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Draw the interface as a box with <<interface>> above the class name and only method signatures inside (no attributes).

Each implementing class uses a dashed line with a hollow arrow pointing to the interface.

If you have an abstract class, write the name in italics and use a solid line with hollow arrow for subclasses. You can mix both: an interface with multiple implementations, one of which is abstract with its own subclasses.

A common mistake is confusing relationship arrows (especially inheritance vs interface implementation) or forgetting that class diagrams show structure, not runtime flow.

sections.title: Relationship Lines at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Inheritance|~IS-A|solid line|hollow triangle|Car --|> Vehicle
violet|Implementation|~implements interface|dashed line|hollow triangle|Car ..|> Parkable
emerald|Composition|~strong owns, part dies|solid line|filled diamond|Lot *-- Floor
amber|Aggregation|~weak owns, part survives|solid line|hollow diamond|Team o-- Player
cyan|Association|~uses / knows|plain line|arrow optional|Order --> Customer

sections.title: Mermaid Class Diagram = the UML in text
sections.content:
```java
// The Java this UML describes:
abstract class Vehicle { String plate; void start(); }   // box: name + attr + method
class Car extends Vehicle implements Parkable { }        // inheritance + implementation
class ParkingLot { List<ParkingFloor> floors; }          // composition (1 -> *)
interface Parkable { boolean park(ParkingSpot s); }      // <<interface>>
```
*Each Java construct maps to one UML element: `extends`→hollow triangle, field-collection→diamond.*

questions.question: How do you show an interface and its implementations in a class diagram?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of interface notation in UML, which is fundamental since well-designed systems use interfaces for loose coupling and dependency inversion.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a solid line instead of dashed for interface implementation, or forgetting the <<interface>> stereotype label, making it look like a regular class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that interfaces typically define behavior contracts (PaymentProcessor, NotificationService) and explain how this enables dependency injection in Spring applications.

questions.direct_answer: Draw the interface as a box with <<interface>> above the class name and only method signatures inside (no attributes). Each implementing class uses a dashed line with a hollow arrow pointing to the interface. If you have an abstract class, write the name in italics and use a solid line with hollow arrow for subclasses. You can mix both: an interface with multiple implementations, one of which is abstract with its own subclasses.

answer_sections.content: In UML, interfaces get the <<interface>> label in the class box and their methods are listed without implementation. A class implementing an interface uses a dashed line with a hollow triangular arrowhead pointing at the interface — it's 'realization' in UML terminology. Abstract classes have their name in italics and abstract methods in italics too. So for pricing: <<interface>> PricingStrategy has +calculateFee(Vehicle, Duration): BigDecimal. Then HourlyPricingStrategy and DailyPricingStrategy both have dashed implementation arrows to PricingStrategy. On a whiteboard I usually write <<interface>> or just 'I' prefix on the box to distinguish from concrete classes — perfect UML syntax matters less than clear communication.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Interface box = **«interface»** label + method signatures only.
- Implementers connect with a **dashed line + hollow triangle** (realization).
- Abstract class name is **italic**; subclasses use a **solid line + triangle** (generalization).
- **Dashed = implements, solid = extends** — the quick tell.
- The triangle always points **to** the interface/parent.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
To show an interface in a class diagram, I draw a box like any class, but I put the interface stereotype — the word interface in guillemets, those double angle brackets — above the name, and inside I list only method signatures, no instance attributes, because an interface has no state. Then each class that implements the interface connects to it with a dashed line and a hollow triangle pointing at the interface. That dashed line is the key signal; in UML it's called realization, and it specifically means implements.

The contrast is with an abstract class. There I write the class name in italics to show it's abstract, and subclasses connect to it with a solid line and a hollow triangle — that's generalization, which means extends. So the quick mental rule is dashed equals implements, solid equals extends, and the triangle always points toward the interface or parent, never away from it.

You can absolutely mix the two in one diagram, which is common in real designs. For a payment example, I might have a PaymentMethod interface with CreditCard and UpiPayment realizing it via dashed arrows, and also an abstract Wallet class that implements PaymentMethod and is itself extended by concrete wallet types using a solid arrow. Reading that diagram, you can instantly see which relationships are contracts being fulfilled and which are code being inherited, purely from whether the line is dashed or solid.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Draw the interface as a box with <<interface>> above the class name and only method signatures inside (no attributes).

Each implementing class uses a dashed line with a hollow arrow pointing to the interface.

If you have an abstract class, write the name in italics and use a solid line with hollow arrow for subclasses. You can mix both: an interface with multiple implementations, one of which is abstract with its own subclasses.

A common mistake is confusing relationship arrows (especially inheritance vs interface implementation) or forgetting that class diagrams show structure, not runtime flow.

sections.title: Java — Interface and Implementations
Interface + Implementations
sections.content:
```mermaid
classDiagram
    class PaymentMethod {
        <<interface>>
        +pay(amount) void
    }
    class CreditCard
    class UpiPayment
    class Wallet {
        <<abstract>>
    }
    class PayPalWallet
    PaymentMethod <|.. CreditCard
    PaymentMethod <|.. UpiPayment
    PaymentMethod <|.. Wallet
    Wallet <|-- PayPalWallet
```
*Dashed (`<|..`) = implements/realization; solid (`<|--`) = extends/generalization.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Solid line for implementation** — `implements` is a *dashed* line; solid is for `extends`.
- **Attributes inside an interface box** — interfaces show methods (and constants), not instance fields.
- **Forgetting the «interface» / italic markers** — without them the reader can't tell the type.
- **Arrow pointing the wrong way** — the triangle points *to* the interface/parent.

questions.question: How much detail should a class diagram in an LLD interview have?

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment about what level of abstraction communicates design effectively in a time-constrained interview setting—shows experience thinking like a designer, not just a coder.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Either creating a nearly blank diagram with just class names and lines (too abstract) or drawing every field and method including constructors and getters (too detailed, wastes time).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explicitly state your detail level choice at the start: 'I'll show the core classes with key fields and methods, skipping standard getters to focus on design decisions.' Then deliver on that promise.

questions.direct_answer: Include all major classes that represent distinct responsibilities, show their important relationships (inheritance, composition, key associations), and list 3-5 critical attributes and methods per class—enough to convey design decisions. Skip getters, setters, utility methods, and minor helper classes. The goal is clarity about architecture, not completeness. If you're spending more than 15 minutes drawing, you have too much detail.

answer_sections.content: The rule for LLD interview diagrams: enough to communicate the design, not a complete specification. I show all major classes and their important relationships. For attributes, I include the fields that capture the key design decisions — like Vehicle having a VehicleType enum field — but not every trivial field. For methods, I show the key public APIs: ParkingLot.findAvailableSpot(), ParkingSpot.occupy() — not the private helpers or getters. The most important things to show are: inheritance hierarchies (abstract Vehicle), composition relationships (filled diamonds), and interfaces (<<interface>> labels). A good diagram tells the story of the design in 3-5 minutes of drawing. If I'm spending 15 minutes drawing, I'm being too detailed.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: The right amount of detail is the amount that fits in fifteen minutes and still shows your design decisions — no more.

beats.text: An interview class diagram should communicate the design clearly in 3 to 5 minutes of drawing. It's a communication tool, not a specification.

groups.heading: Always include
groups.text: All major classes, inheritance hierarchies, composition relationships, and interfaces. These are the design decisions — they must be visible.

groups.heading: Include selectively
groups.text: Key attributes that reflect design choices (VehicleType enum field, boolean isOccupied) and key public methods (findAvailableSpot, occupy, free).

groups.heading: Skip entirely
groups.text: Getters, setters, private helpers, trivial fields. They add clutter without communicating design.

beats.text: Draw the diagram alongside your verbal explanation, not before and not after. Narrate each box and arrow as you draw it — the interviewer is following your reasoning, not just your pen.
sharp edge: if you're spending more than 10 minutes on the diagram, you're too detailed. Step back, focus on relationships and key design decisions only.

speakable_v2.cap: Show what's abstract, what's an interface, and how things compose or inherit. Skip getters and setters. A clean 5-minute diagram beats an exhaustive 15-minute one every time.

sections.title: How Much Detail Belongs in an LLD Diagram
sections.content:
An interview class diagram should convey **design decisions, not completeness**. Include every class that represents a **distinct responsibility**, show the **important relationships** (inheritance, composition, key associations), and list **3–5 critical attributes and methods** per class.

**Skip** getters, setters, trivial helpers, and minor utility classes — they add ink without adding insight. The pragmatic signal: if you've spent more than ~15 minutes on the diagram, you're over-detailing. A reader should grasp the architecture in seconds.

sections.title: How Much Detail at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Always include|~The design decisions|major classes|inheritance + composition|interfaces
emerald|Include selectively|~3-5 per class|key attributes|key public methods|enums for state
amber|Skip entirely|~Just clutter|getters/setters|private helpers|framework classes
rose|Time signal|~A communication tool|aim for 3-5 minutes|> 15 min = too detailed|legible at a glance

sections.title: Include vs Skip
sections.content:
| Include | Skip |
|---|---|
| Classes with distinct responsibilities | Trivial utility/helper classes |
| Inheritance, composition, key associations | Every minor association |
| 3–5 key attributes per class | Getters, setters, `toString` |
| Important method signatures | Private helper methods |
| Multiplicities (1, \*) | Exact parameter lists everywhere |
| Enums for states/types | Framework/library classes |

sections.title: Right-Sized Class Sketch
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Listing every getter/setter** — clutters the box and hides the design.
- **Drawing framework classes** — `List`, `Optional`, Spring types aren't your design.
- **Over-detailing parameters** — signatures convey intent; exhaustive params don't.
- **Spending 20+ minutes on the diagram** — leave time for trade-offs and code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Show **design decisions, not completeness**.
- Include classes with **distinct responsibilities** + key relationships.
- **3–5 key attributes/methods** per class; skip getters/setters/helpers.
- Add **multiplicities** and enums for states.
- If it takes **>15 minutes**, you're over-detailing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The guiding principle is that an interview class diagram exists to convey design decisions, not to be a complete code listing. So I include every class that represents a distinct responsibility, I show the important relationships — inheritance, composition, and the key associations — and inside each box I put maybe three to five of the most critical attributes and methods. That's enough for someone to understand the architecture and the choices I made.

What I deliberately leave out is just as important. I skip getters and setters, trivial helpers, toString and equals, and minor utility classes, because they fill the diagram with ink that hides the actual design. I also don't draw framework or library classes like List or Optional — those aren't my design, they're just plumbing. And I don't agonise over exact parameter lists; a method name and its intent usually communicate enough.

The practical signal I use is time. If I've spent more than about fifteen minutes drawing, I've gone too deep, because the diagram is a means to an end, and I need to leave time to write some key class skeletons and discuss trade-offs and extensibility. A reader should be able to glance at the diagram and grasp the structure in seconds. Five meaningful members per class beats fifty exhaustive ones every time — clarity about the architecture is the goal, not completeness.

questions.question: How do you draw a class diagram for a simple parking lot on a whiteboard?

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to translate a real-world system into a class diagram on the spot, under time pressure, which is the core of LLD interview rounds.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Either drawing too many classes with every possible detail (wasting time) or drawing only entity names without showing relationships and key members.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain your design choices aloud while drawing—why Vehicle is abstract, why you chose composition for floors, and how the ticket links vehicle to spot for billing.

questions.direct_answer: Start by identifying the main entities: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, Vehicle (with Car/Motorcycle subclasses), ParkingTicket, and a fee calculator. Draw a box for each with 3-5 key attributes and methods. Then connect them: ParkingLot contains multiple ParkingFloors (composition), each floor has multiple ParkingSpots (composition), Vehicle is abstract with inheritance arrows to concrete types, and ParkingTicket associates with Vehicle and ParkingSpot.

answer_sections.content: For a whiteboard class diagram, I start with the core entities and their relationships. I draw ParkingLot at the top with a composition arrow to ParkingFloor (filled diamond), ParkingFloor with composition to ParkingSpot. Vehicle is drawn as abstract in italics with Car and Motorcycle below it connected by inheritance arrows. ParkingTicket has association lines to both Vehicle (it references) and ParkingSpot (it's for). FeeCalculator is a separate box with dependency line from ParkingLot. I add key attributes and methods in each box, focusing on the important ones rather than being exhaustive. The diagram should tell the story of how the system works without needing explanation.

ParkingFloor with a filled diamond down to ParkingSpot
Vehicle as abstract (write name in italics), with Car and Motorcycle below it via inheritance arrows

non-obvious: the diagram should tell the story on its own without needing explanation. If you finish drawing and the interviewer can't read the design at a glance, you've added too much noise or missed a key relationship.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Lay out **top-down by ownership**: lot → floor → spot.
- 3–5 key attributes/methods per box; skip getters/setters.
- **Composition diamonds** down the chain; **inheritance triangles** for vehicles.
- Diamond sits on the **owner** end.
- Label **multiplicities** (1, \*).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
On a whiteboard I start by listing the main entities so I don't forget any: ParkingLot, ParkingFloor, ParkingSpot, the Vehicle hierarchy with Car and Motorcycle, and ParkingTicket. Then the layout trick that keeps the diagram clean is to arrange boxes by ownership, top to bottom. I put ParkingLot at the top, ParkingFloor underneath it, and ParkingSpot under that, with the Vehicle hierarchy off to one side. That way the composition lines all flow downward and don't cross each other.

In each box I write three to five of the most important attributes and methods — enough to convey the design decisions — and I deliberately skip getters, setters, and trivial helpers, because they add clutter without adding meaning. Then I draw the relationships. ParkingLot to ParkingFloor and ParkingFloor to ParkingSpot are composition, so I use a solid line with a filled diamond on the owner's end, since a spot can't exist without its floor. For the vehicles, Car and Motorcycle inherit from the abstract Vehicle, so I draw solid lines with hollow triangles pointing up to Vehicle.

Finally I annotate multiplicities — a one next to the lot and a star next to the floors — so anyone reading it instantly sees the one-to-many. The whole point is that a clean diagram with correct arrowheads and multiplicities communicates the design faster than any amount of talking, so I keep it tidy and let the notation do the work.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Draw the interface as a box with <<interface>> above the class name and only method signatures inside (no attributes).

Each implementing class uses a dashed line with a hollow arrow pointing to the interface.

If you have an abstract class, write the name in italics and use a solid line with hollow arrow for subclasses. You can mix both: an interface with multiple implementations, one of which is abstract with its own subclasses.

A common mistake is confusing relationship arrows (especially inheritance vs interface implementation) or forgetting that class diagrams show structure, not runtime flow.

sections.title: Whiteboard Steps
sections.content:
| Step | Do this |
|---|---|
| 1 | List entities: `ParkingLot`, `ParkingFloor`, `ParkingSpot`, `Vehicle`, `Car`, `ParkingTicket` |
| 2 | Place owners on top, parts below (lot → floor → spot) |
| 3 | Put 3–5 key fields + methods in each box; skip getters/setters |
| 4 | Draw composition (filled diamond) down the ownership chain |
| 5 | Draw inheritance triangles for `Car`/`Motorcycle` → `Vehicle` |
| 6 | Add multiplicities (1, \*) on each line |

The Whiteboard Result

```mermaid

    class ParkingLot { +park(v) }
    class ParkingFloor { +findFree(size) }
    class ParkingSpot { -SpotSize size }
    class Vehicle { -String plate }
    class Car
    class Motorcycle
    ParkingLot "1" *-- "*" ParkingFloor
    ParkingFloor "1" *-- "*" ParkingSpot
    Vehicle <|-- Car
    Vehicle <|-- Motorcycle
    ParkingSpot --> Vehicle : holds
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Cramming every method** into boxes — show 3–5 that convey design; skip getters.
- **Tangled lines** — lay out by ownership (top-down) to keep composition lines clean.
- **Wrong diamond direction** — the filled diamond sits on the *owner* (lot), not the part.
- **Forgetting multiplicities** — `1` and `*` communicate the one-to-many at a glance.
